meta.title: The Promotion War
meta.subtitle: How to win the ladder when someone else wants your rung
meta.description: A closed file on workplace advancement. How decisions about your promotion actually get made, who makes them in the room you are not in, and what to do about the rival who is already ahead of you. Twenty-five cards of field moves — sponsor capture, credit control, rival containment, and the endgame after you win.
meta.author: AI

cards.title: Find Out Who Actually Decides Your Promotion
cards.principle: Pfeffer: Rule 3 — Build Power by Understanding the Real Org Chart
cards.remember: Your boss recommends. Someone else approves. Learn that name.
cards.when: You are working hard for your boss and assuming they can promote you.
cards.hook: Your boss cannot promote you alone. Somebody upstairs signs it, and they have never heard your name.
cards.truth:
Promotions get decided in a room with eight people and a spreadsheet.
• Your boss puts your name on a list and defends it for ninety seconds.
• The other seven people vote on a reputation you did not build with them.
• Most people spend a year impressing the one person who cannot decide.
cards.theySee: A person who asks smart questions about how the company works, not a person who wants something.

signals.t: Your boss disappears into a long meeting every quarter and comes back tired
Someone mentions a talent review or a calibration meeting
Your boss says the decision is above them but will not say whose
A peer got promoted and nobody on your team saw it coming

steps.title: Ask your boss who else votes
steps.desc: Say you want to understand the process. Ask which other leaders are in the room.

steps.title: Write the list of names
steps.desc: Write every name down. Mark who has met you and who has not.

steps.title: Get one meeting with one stranger
steps.desc: Ask your boss to introduce you to one name on the list this month.

cards.script: "I want to be useful for longer here, so I want to understand the process. When my level comes up, who is in the room besides you? I would rather learn that now than the week before."
cards.example: Devon assumed his director controlled his promotion. He asked once and learned five VPs voted. Three had never met him. He got introduced to two of them over the next quarter and made the list the following cycle.
cards.watchFor: Your boss starts naming people and explaining what each one cares about.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss dodges and says "just focus on your work." That is a signal, not an answer — they either do not know or do not want you talking upward. Go sideways instead: ask a recently promoted peer who interviewed them for the level. Say: "You just went through this. Who did you end up having to convince?"
cards.counter:
If someone keeps you focused only on your own tasks, they are keeping you off the map.
• Notice when every answer about promotion points back to them alone.
• Say: "Who else weighs in? I want to meet them early."
• Build one relationship above your boss this quarter, quietly.
cards.insight: Knowing the room is cheap. The harder part is that once you know the names, you cannot un-know that you are a stranger to most of them — and you have maybe nine months to fix that.

cards.title: Find the Job Nobody Wants But Everyone Watches
cards.principle: Pfeffer: Rule 1 — Get Out of Your Own Way × Resource Dependence
cards.remember: Take the ugly project everyone important is watching.
cards.when: Your team has a broken project and nobody will put their hand up to own it.
cards.hook: Safe work makes you competent. Broken work makes you known.
cards.truth:
Leaders remember whoever stood next to the fire, win or lose.
• A broken project has senior attention already attached to it.
• Nobody expects a fix, so any progress reads as a big win.
• The trap is picking a project that is broken because it has no money or no power behind it.
cards.theySee: A person volunteering for the thing that made everyone else look at their shoes.

signals.t: A VP mentions the project by name in two different meetings
The room goes quiet when your boss asks who will own it
The project has already had two owners in a year
The project still has money and headcount attached to it

steps.title: Check who watches it
steps.desc: Ask if any VP reports on this project. If no senior person asks about it, skip it.

steps.title: Ask for the fix, not the job
steps.desc: Tell your boss you will take it for ninety days with a clear target.

steps.title: Send a status note upward in week two
steps.desc: Write five lines: what was broken, what you changed, what you need. Copy the VP who cares.

cards.script: "I will take the migration. Ninety days, and I will report the number every two weeks. If it is still broken at day ninety, you can hand it to someone else and I will not argue."
cards.example: Priya took the billing project that had burned two managers. She cut the error rate from 9% to 1.2% in eleven weeks and sent a two-line update to the CFO every Friday. She was promoted in the next cycle over a peer with better reviews.
cards.watchFor: A senior leader replies to your update email directly instead of through your boss.
cards.ifItFails: The project is worse than advertised and you are sinking. Do not go quiet — silence is how owners three and four died. Report the real number early and name the thing you cannot fix: "The error rate is stuck at 4% because two teams own the same table. I need you to pick one owner by Friday." Now the blocker belongs to them.
cards.counter:
If your boss pushes a broken project at you and nobody senior is watching, they are dumping.
• Ask who reports on it upward and how often. Silence is your answer.
• Say: "Who sees the results of this? I want to send them updates directly."
• If nobody senior cares, pass. Do not use this on a project with no budget.
cards.insight: Visible failure beats invisible success, but only inside a limit. The real question is how many quarters you can run hot before you need one clean win to prove you finish things.

cards.title: Learn the Exact Words They Use for Your Level
cards.principle: Cialdini: Consistency × Institutional Script Matching
cards.remember: Speak their promotion language back to them word for word.
cards.when: You keep hearing you are doing great work but you are not moving up.
cards.hook: Every company has five words that unlock a level. If you do not say them, you did not qualify.
cards.truth:
Promotion committees run on a written rubric and a tired reader.
• The reader scans your packet for the exact words in the rubric.
• Your accomplishments in your own words score as "unclear scope."
• Most people describe what they did. The winners describe it in the company's vocabulary.
cards.theySee: A person whose work sounds like it already belongs at the next level.

signals.t: HR has a leveling document nobody on your team has opened
Your skip-level uses the same phrase three times a month
Feedback says your impact was unclear even though the project shipped
A promoted peer's write-up uses phrases you have never used

steps.title: Get the leveling document
steps.desc: Ask HR or your boss for the written criteria for the next level. Read it twice.

steps.title: Underline the repeated verbs
steps.desc: Mark every verb that appears more than once. Those are the words that score.

steps.title: Rewrite your last three wins in those words
steps.desc: Send the rewritten version to your boss as your quarterly update.

cards.script: "Can you send me the written criteria for the next level? I want to check my last quarter against it line by line and tell you where the gaps are before you have to."
cards.example: Marcus shipped two systems and got told his "scope was unclear." He read the rubric, found the phrase "drove cross-team alignment," and rewrote the same two projects using it. Same work, same year. He got the level.
cards.watchFor: Your boss copies your sentences into their own write-up without changing them.
cards.ifItFails: There is no written rubric, or HR will not share it. Then build it from evidence: ask two recently promoted people to send you their packets. Say: "You just got through it. Can I read your write-up? I want to see what a passing one looks like." A real example beats a policy document anyway.
cards.counter:
If someone praises your work but never uses level language about it, you are being kept comfortable.
• Notice praise that is warm and vague: "great job," "real rock star."
• Say: "Against the criteria for the next level, where am I short?"
• Make them answer in the rubric's words or admit there is no plan.
cards.insight: The rubric is a translation problem, not a merit problem. What follows is harder: once you speak the language fluently, you find out whether the gap was ever really about your work.

cards.title: Count the Open Slots Before You Compete
cards.principle: Sun Tzu: Know the Ground — Terrain Before Tactics
cards.remember: Check how many spots exist before you fight for one.
cards.when: You and two strong peers are all clearly going for the same level.
cards.hook: You can win every argument and still lose because there was only one chair. Count chairs first.
cards.truth:
Most promotion budgets are fixed before anyone is evaluated.
• Finance sets a number of slots per team, per cycle, months in advance.
• Your performance decides your rank, not whether a slot exists.
• The move is not to outwork rivals. It is to find the team with a spare chair.
cards.theySee: A person asking practical questions about budget and headcount, like a manager would.

signals.t: Only one person on your team got promoted in each of the last two cycles
Your boss mentions a hiring pause or a flat headcount plan
Three people at your level all have strong reviews
Another team just lost someone at the level you want

steps.title: Ask how many slots your team gets
steps.desc: Ask your boss directly how many promotions the team can fund this cycle.

steps.title: Count the people ahead of you
steps.desc: List peers at your level with strong reviews. That is your real queue.

steps.title: Look at one other team
steps.desc: Find a team with a vacancy at your target level. Ask for coffee with that manager.

cards.script: "Straight question, no drama: how many promotions can this team fund this cycle? If the answer is one and Aisha is ahead of me, I would rather know now and plan around it."
cards.example: Tom found out his team had one slot and his peer had a two-year head start. He moved to the platform team, which had lost a senior engineer and had funded backfill. He was promoted eight months later instead of waiting three years.
cards.watchFor: Your boss hesitates, then gives you a number instead of a speech.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss will not give a number and calls the question inappropriate. Do not push them twice. Go around: ask a friendly recruiter or a finance partner how the headcount plan works. Then say to your boss: "I hear the plan funds one at my level. If that is right, tell me where I sit in the order."
cards.counter:
If a manager keeps you competing hard for a slot that does not exist, they are farming your effort.
• Notice years of "almost there" with no peer ever promoted.
• Say: "How many people at my level has this team promoted in three years?"
• If the answer is zero, the problem is the chair, not you. Move teams.
cards.insight: Changing ground beats fighting harder on bad ground. The cost is that you restart your reputation from scratch, and the clock on a new team runs about two quarters before anyone will back you.

cards.title: Get a Sponsor, Not Another Mentor
cards.principle: Hewlett: Sponsorship vs Mentorship × Pfeffer: Rule 4 — Build a Network
cards.remember: A mentor talks to you. A sponsor talks about you.
cards.when: You have people who give you career advice but nobody who fights for you.
cards.hook: Advice is free because it costs the giver nothing. You need somebody who will spend their own credit on your name.
cards.truth:
A sponsor is a senior person who will lose something if you fail.
• They argue for you in the room while you are not there.
• They only do it if backing you makes them look smart.
• Most people collect mentors, who feel good and change nothing.
cards.theySee: A person solving a problem the senior leader personally owns.

signals.t: Your mentor gives you great advice and has never mentioned you to anyone
A senior leader requests you by name for a piece of work
Someone senior repeats your idea in a meeting and says your name
A leader pushed back when someone criticized your work

steps.title: Pick one leader with a live problem
steps.desc: Find a senior person with a public goal that is behind. Read their last update.

steps.title: Deliver something they did not ask for
steps.desc: Solve one small piece of their problem and send it in under a page.

steps.title: Ask them to use you again
steps.desc: Say you want more of this work. Do not ask for sponsorship yet.

cards.script: "I saw the onboarding number is stuck at 40%. I pulled the drop-off data and found two screens causing half of it. One page attached. If it is useful, I would like to fix it."
cards.example: Nadia noticed a VP's retention target was missing by 12 points. She sent him a one-page teardown he never asked for. Three weeks later he pulled her into his staff meeting, and at the next talent review he argued for her level himself.
cards.watchFor: They forward your work to someone else with your name at the top.
cards.ifItFails: They take your work and say nothing. Do not send a second gift — that reads as need. Ask for a small return instead, one that costs them almost nothing but puts your name in their mouth: "Would you introduce me to Dana? You mentioned she owns the next phase." A referral is the first real test of sponsorship.
cards.counter:
If a senior person keeps giving you advice and never your name, you are their hobby, not their bet.
• Notice long coffees with zero introductions after six months.
• Say: "What would you need to see before you would back me for the next level?"
• If the answer stays vague twice, stop investing. Find someone with a problem.
cards.insight: Sponsors buy you with their own reputation, which means they need you to win publicly. The next problem is that you now owe them, and the bill usually arrives as a job you did not want.

cards.title: Make Your Boss Look Good to Their Boss
cards.principle: Greene: Law 1 — Never Outshine the Master
cards.remember: Feed your boss wins they can carry upstairs with their name on them.
cards.when: Your boss controls the first vote on your promotion and cares about their own standing.
cards.hook: Your boss is not judging your work. They are judging what your work does to their reputation.
cards.truth:
Your manager gets measured by their team's results, not your talent.
• Give them a number they can say out loud in their own review.
• They start defending you because your win is their win.
• The trap is doing it so loudly it looks like you want their job.
cards.theySee: A person who hands them a clean result they can report upward without editing.

signals.t: Your boss asks for metrics right before their skip-level meeting
They get tense on the day of their leadership review
Your framing shows up in their slides word for word
They start asking what you need from them

steps.title: Find out what they get measured on
steps.desc: Ask which three numbers their boss asks them about every month.

steps.title: Move one of those numbers
steps.desc: Pick the one you can touch. Change it and record the before and after.

steps.title: Hand it over the day before their review
steps.desc: Send two lines with the number and the cause. Say it is for their update.

cards.script: "Before your review tomorrow — ticket backlog is down from 210 to 74 since March. Cause was the triage rule change. Use it however you want, no need to mention me."
cards.example: Sam learned his director was measured on deploy frequency. He automated one release step and pushed weekly deploys from 3 to 11. He handed the number over the night before the director's review. The director named him unprompted at the next talent meeting.
cards.watchFor: They start telling the story upward themselves, using your exact numbers.
cards.ifItFails: They take the number and never mention you anywhere. Stop giving gifts and start creating a record. Put the next number in a written update that goes to both your boss and their boss, with the work attributed once, flatly: "Recap for the thread: triage rule change, backlog 210 to 74, shipped by me and Chen."
cards.counter:
If someone keeps handing you wins and asking for nothing, they are building a debt.
• Notice a peer who is generous with credit and quiet about their goal.
• Say: "This helps me. What do you want out of this quarter?"
• Pay it back small and early. An unpaid debt is what they will spend later.
cards.insight: Making your boss look good works right up to the moment they realize you could replace them. The next card in this file is the one about what to do when they start slowing you down.

cards.title: Build a Second Line to Your Skip-Level
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — Do Not Depend on One Patron
cards.remember: One boss is a single point of failure. Build a second door.
cards.when: Your entire career depends on one manager's opinion of you.
cards.hook: Managers leave, get fired, or turn on you. If your name only lives in one person's mouth, you are one reorg from invisible.
cards.truth:
A single channel to power is a channel someone else can close.
• A skip-level relationship gives your name a second route into the room.
• Your boss becomes one voice among several, not the gate.
• Do it clumsily and it reads as going around them. Then they fight you.
cards.theySee: A person their skip-level already knows and speaks well of, which is awkward to argue with.

signals.t: Your boss forwards your updates upward instead of letting you present
They say the skip-level is too busy for a short meeting
Your skip-level mentions a detail about your work you never told them
People start talking about a team restructure

steps.title: Ask your boss to open the door
steps.desc: Ask them to introduce you. Doing it through them removes the threat.

steps.title: Bring one problem, not a resume
steps.desc: In the meeting, ask about their biggest blocker. Do not sell yourself.

steps.title: Send one short follow-up a month
steps.desc: Three lines on the thing they cared about. Copy your boss every time.

cards.script: (To your boss) "I want to understand what Priya's team is chasing this year so I stop guessing. Would you set up twenty minutes with the three of us, and then I will keep her posted on the migration directly with you copied?"
cards.example: Rachel's director blocked her from senior meetings for a year. She asked him to introduce her to his VP for a single project sync, then sent the VP a three-line update monthly with her director copied. When her director left, the VP already had a view of her and moved her up in the same cycle.
cards.watchFor: Your skip-level replies to your update directly and asks a follow-up question.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss refuses the introduction and gets cold about it. Stop asking — you have your answer, and now you know your boss is the obstacle. Use neutral ground instead: join a cross-team working group your skip-level attends. Say in that room: "I own the migration piece. I will send a weekly note to this group." Now the channel exists and nobody granted it.
cards.counter:
If your manager insists all communication upward goes through them, you are being contained.
• Notice that you never present your own work to their boss.
• Say: "I would like to present this piece myself next time. Same slides."
• Do not use this on a manager who signs your review and already distrusts you. Wait for a project that needs a cross-team room.
cards.insight: Two channels beat one, and three beat two. The harder problem is keeping your boss comfortable while you build them, because a manager who feels bypassed will move against you before your second channel is strong.

cards.title: Ask for a Favor to Make Them Like You
cards.principle: Cialdini: Consistency × The Benjamin Franklin Effect
cards.remember: Ask a busy senior person for a small favor. They invest in you.
cards.when: You need a senior leader to notice you and you have nothing to offer them yet.
cards.hook: You cannot win over a powerful stranger by being useful — they have a hundred useful people. Get them to spend five minutes on you instead.
cards.truth:
People trust whoever they have already invested in.
• A small favor makes them explain their own choice to themselves.
• Their brain settles on: I helped that one because they are worth helping.
• Ask too big and it reverses. Then you are a cost, not an investment.
cards.theySee: A person who values their opinion enough to ask for it, and who came prepared.

signals.t: They agreed to a short meeting without pushing it out a month
They marked up your document instead of saying it looked fine
They ask you later how the thing they advised turned out
They describe you to someone else as "someone I have been helping"

steps.title: Pick a favor that costs ten minutes
steps.desc: Ask them to review one page or answer one specific question. Nothing bigger.

steps.title: Make it about their expertise
steps.desc: Name the exact reason you asked them and not somebody else.

steps.title: Report back what you did with it
steps.desc: Within two weeks, tell them what changed because of their advice.

cards.script: "You built the pricing model everyone still uses. I have a one-page proposal and I keep second-guessing the assumptions. Would you spend ten minutes marking up the ugly parts?"
cards.example: Leo asked a distant VP to review one page on pricing assumptions. She sent back four comments. He implemented three and emailed her the result two weeks later. She started copying him on strategy threads and later put his name forward for a stretch role.
cards.watchFor: They give you more time than you asked for and start telling you a story about their own career.
cards.ifItFails: They ignore the ask or send back one word. Do not chase and do not apologize. Close the loop anyway a month later with the result — that costs them nothing and puts you back in view: "You did not need to reply, but I shipped the change we talked about and it moved conversion 4 points. Thank you." People answer a thank-you they did not earn.
cards.counter:
If a junior person keeps asking you for small favors, they are building a claim on you.
• Notice the pattern: little asks, warm follow-ups, growing familiarity.
• Say: "Happy to. What are you actually going for here?"
• Decide once whether you want to back them. Do not drift into it.
cards.insight: Getting help makes people like you more than giving help does. The next question is what you do when they finally ask for something back and it is not convenient.

cards.title: Send the Weekly Note Nobody Asked For
cards.principle: Zajonc: Mere Exposure × Availability Heuristic
cards.remember: A short weekly update makes people remember you when it counts.
cards.when: You do good work but senior people cannot describe what you do.
cards.hook: At promotion time, they can only argue for what they remember. Memory is built weekly, not in one big presentation.
cards.truth:
Decision makers back the name that comes to mind fastest.
• A five-line weekly note puts your name in their inbox 50 times a year.
• They begin to feel they know your work without ever reviewing it.
• The trap is writing a long status report. Nobody reads past line six.
cards.theySee: A person who is organized, low-maintenance, and always shipping something.

signals.t: A senior leader describes your job incorrectly in a meeting
Your project gets praised and someone else's name is attached
Someone replies to your note with a question about line three
You hear your own phrasing repeated in a meeting you were not in

steps.title: Write five lines every Friday
steps.desc: Shipped, numbers, blocked, next week, one ask. Nothing else.

steps.title: Send it to three people
steps.desc: Your boss, your skip-level, and one leader in another team who touches your work.

steps.title: Keep every one in a folder
steps.desc: At review time you have a dated record instead of a memory.

cards.script: "Friday note. Shipped: new triage rule, live Wednesday. Number: backlog 210 → 74. Blocked: need a decision on data owner. Next: auto-routing. Ask: ten minutes with you Tuesday."
cards.example: Elena sent a five-line Friday note to her VP for seven months. She never asked for anything big. In the promotion meeting, the VP was the one who said "she has been running that migration since March" — the only person in the room who could describe her work.
cards.watchFor: Someone quotes a line from your note back to you weeks later.
cards.ifItFails: Nobody replies for a month and you feel foolish. Silence is not failure here — inbox presence works without replies. But add one hook: put a real question in the ask line that only they can answer. "Ask: do you want auto-routing before or after the audit? I will go with your call." A decision request gets answered when a status update does not.
cards.counter:
If a peer sends constant updates upward, they are building a record you do not have.
• Notice whose name leaders use when describing shared work.
• Say in the shared channel: "Adding to that — I owned the routing piece."
• Start your own note the same week. Do not complain about theirs.
cards.insight: Being remembered beats being right. The harder part is that once leaders can describe your work, they start assigning you more of the same — and you have to steer what they remember, not just how often.

cards.title: Take Credit in the Room Without Sounding Like It
cards.principle: Pfeffer: Rule 5 — Make Your Power Visible
cards.remember: Say what you did in one flat sentence. Then stop talking.
cards.when: Your work gets praised in a meeting and nobody says your name.
cards.hook: Modesty is a tax you pay to people who will not pay you back. State the fact and move on.
cards.truth:
Credit gets assigned by whoever speaks first, not by who did the work.
• A flat factual sentence sets the record without triggering the room.
• People accept plain facts. They resist a story about how hard you worked.
• The trap is over-explaining. Length signals insecurity and invites doubt.
cards.theySee: A person calmly adding a fact, not a person defending themselves.

signals.t: Someone says the project "got done" with no name attached
A peer summarizes your work at the top of the meeting
A leader thanks the wrong person for your result
Your solo work keeps getting described as "the team's"

steps.title: Prepare one sentence before the meeting
steps.desc: Write it out: what you built, the number, done. Under fifteen words.

steps.title: Say it right after the praise lands
steps.desc: Do not wait for a gap. Add it directly onto the compliment.

steps.title: Hand credit to one other person
steps.desc: Name someone real who helped. It stops you sounding like you are grabbing.

cards.script: "Glad it landed. I built the routing layer, Chen did the tests. Next thing on it is the audit — I will bring numbers Thursday."
cards.example: Anika's director praised "the team" for a launch she had built alone over six weeks. She said nine words: "I built the pipeline, Raj ran the rollout." The director corrected himself in the follow-up email. Two peers copied the move within a month.
cards.watchFor: The senior person writes your name down or repeats it back in the same meeting.
cards.ifItFails: Someone talks over you or says "well, it was really a group effort." Do not fight it in the room. Put it in writing within the hour, where written records outrank memory: send the recap to the same group with the split named once, no complaint. "Recap for the thread: routing layer — me, tests — Chen, rollout — Raj. Audit numbers Thursday."
cards.counter:
If a peer states credit flatly and fast, they are setting the record before you can.
• Notice who speaks in the first ten seconds after praise.
• Say: "Right, and I owned the piece that fed into that."
• Speak within the same minute. After the meeting, it is already lost.
cards.insight: Facts stated once win. Facts stated twice sound like a complaint. The real trap is the person who never grabs credit loudly but always writes the recap email — that person is beating you quietly.

cards.title: Own the Recap Email After Every Meeting
cards.principle: Schelling: Focal Point × Documentation as Power
cards.remember: Whoever writes the summary decides what happened.
cards.when: Decisions in your meetings keep getting remembered differently later.
cards.hook: Meetings are noise. The email after the meeting is the only version anybody will read again.
cards.truth:
The written record beats everyone's memory within about three days.
• You choose which decisions were made and who owns what.
• Nobody argues with a recap unless it hurts them directly.
• Do it fairly the first ten times. Then nobody questions the eleventh.
cards.theySee: A person being helpful and organized, saving everyone the work of remembering.

signals.t: Two people leave the same meeting with different conclusions
Nobody takes notes and the action items evaporate
The same question gets argued again two weeks later
Someone forwards your recap to their own boss

steps.title: Send it within one hour
steps.desc: Speed decides whose version becomes the record. Beat everyone else.

steps.title: List decisions and owners only
steps.desc: Three decisions, three names, three dates. Skip the discussion.

steps.title: Include your own name as owner once
steps.desc: Attach yourself to the decision you want associated with your level.

cards.script: "Recap so we do not redo this: 1) We ship auto-routing first — I own it, Oct 3. 2) Audit moves to Q4 — Dana owns. 3) No decision yet on data ownership. Shout if I got any of it wrong."
cards.example: Julian started sending recaps after a weekly cross-team sync where decisions kept reversing. Within two months, three other teams cited his emails as the source of record. When a dispute reached the VP, the VP asked "what did Julian's recap say?"
cards.watchFor: People start quoting your recap in later meetings instead of arguing from memory.
cards.ifItFails: A senior person edits your recap to remove your name or shift ownership. Do not re-edit it back — you will lose that fight publicly. Take the next meeting instead: volunteer to run the agenda. "I will put the agenda together and send the recap after. Send me items by Monday." Agenda control beats recap control.
cards.counter:
If someone always sends the recap, they control what the company remembers.
• Notice a recap where your contribution turned into "the team."
• Reply to the whole thread within the hour: "One correction — I owned the routing piece."
• Correct fast and once. A late correction reads as sour.
cards.insight: Written records beat spoken ones, and fast records beat accurate ones. The next problem is that once you own the record, everyone reads your bias in it — and one obviously self-serving recap burns all the ones before it.

cards.title: Present Your Own Work to the People Above You
cards.principle: Pfeffer: Rule 5 — Make Power Visible × Direct Exposure
cards.remember: Never let someone else present the work you did.
cards.when: Your boss presents your project to leadership and you stay in your seat.
cards.hook: Every layer between you and the decision maker is a layer that can erase you. Get in the room.
cards.truth:
Leaders promote people they have watched handle pressure.
• Presenting shows judgment, not just output. Nobody can relay that.
• Ten minutes in front of a VP outweighs a year of good reviews.
• The trap is asking for stage time instead of offering to save your boss work.
cards.theySee: A manager getting an offer to hand off a slide they did not want to prepare.

signals.t: Your boss presents your slides and answers questions about your work
Your boss cannot answer a detailed question and says they will follow up
You are not on the invite for the review of your own project
A VP emails you directly instead of going through your boss

steps.title: Offer to take one slide
steps.desc: Tell your boss you will present the technical slide so they can focus on the rest.

steps.title: Rehearse the two hardest questions
steps.desc: Write the two worst questions and your answers. Say them out loud once.

steps.title: Answer short and stop
steps.desc: Give the number and the reason in two sentences. Do not fill silence.

cards.script: "You have six slides for Thursday. I will take the migration one so you do not have to prep it — I can answer the detail questions live. You keep the framing and the ask."
cards.example: Karim's manager always presented his work. He offered to take one slide off her plate for a quarterly review. He answered a hard question from the CTO in two sentences. The CTO asked for him by name on the next project.
cards.watchFor: A senior leader asks you a follow-up question directly instead of asking your boss.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss says no and keeps the whole deck. Do not argue about fairness. Make yourself the required attendee instead: "Then I should be in the room for the Q&A — the data questions will come to me anyway and you should not have to take them." Being in the room is 80% of it. Do not run this on a boss who already feels threatened by you; wait for a review where they are underwater on prep.
cards.counter:
If your manager always presents your work and never brings you, they are farming your output.
• Notice you are missing from meetings about projects you own.
• Say: "I will take the detail questions in the room so you do not have to."
• If they refuse twice, they are protecting their position, not the agenda. Plan a move.
cards.insight: Ten minutes of exposure beats a year of quiet delivery. What comes next is harder: once they see you, they compare you to the person one level up, and that comparison starts whether you are ready or not.

cards.title: Work Out What Your Rival Actually Wants
cards.principle: Sun Tzu: Know Your Enemy × Greene: Law 43 — Work on Hearts and Minds
cards.remember: Find out what your rival wants. It may not be your job.
cards.when: A strong peer is clearly competing with you for the same level.
cards.hook: You assume they want what you want. Half the time they want something you would happily give them.
cards.truth:
Most rivalries are accidents of assumption, not real conflicts.
• Learn their actual goal: money, title, a specific team, or a visa.
• If their goal differs from yours, you can trade instead of fight.
• The trap is fighting a two-year war over a chair they never wanted.
cards.theySee: A peer being unusually direct and curious about their plans, not their weaknesses.

signals.t: They keep volunteering for work that does not lead to your level
They mention pay bands more than titles
They talk about another team's work with obvious interest
They mention a visa, a move, or a personal deadline

steps.title: Ask them directly over lunch
steps.desc: Ask what they want in two years. Most people answer honestly when asked plainly.

steps.title: Compare their answer to yours
steps.desc: Write both goals side by side. Mark where they actually collide.

steps.title: Offer a trade if they do not
steps.desc: Give them the piece they want. Take the piece that maps to your level.

cards.script: "Straight question. What do you actually want in two years — the title, the money, or a different kind of work? I am asking because I would rather we split the work than trip over each other."
cards.example: Grace assumed Ben was after her manager role. Over lunch he said he wanted to move into data science and cared mostly about pay. She gave him the analytics workstream and took the people-leading one. Both got promoted in the same cycle, different tracks.
cards.watchFor: They answer in specifics — a number, a team name, a date — instead of a vague ambition.
cards.ifItFails: They give you a smooth non-answer and stay competitive. Now you know it is real. Stop sharing information with them and watch what they volunteer for — that is the honest answer. Say to your boss instead: "Ben and I are both aiming at the same level. I would rather you split our scope clearly than have us overlap." Let the split come from above.
cards.counter:
If a rival asks you what you want, they are mapping your goal to plan around it.
• Notice a friendly peer asking career questions and sharing nothing back.
• Say: "Depends on the year. What are you going for?"
• Answer one level less specific than they did. Make them go first.
cards.insight: Most rivals are not enemies, just people standing near your chair. The harder case is the one who wants exactly what you want and is better at this than you — that is the next section of this file.

cards.title: Let Your Strongest Rival Take the Doomed Project
cards.principle: Greene: Law 7 — Get Others to Do the Work × Sun Tzu: Attack Where They Cannot Defend
cards.remember: Point your rival at the project that cannot succeed.
cards.when: A high-visibility project is quietly unwinnable and your rival wants attention.
cards.hook: You do not have to beat a strong rival. You just have to be somewhere else when they lose.
cards.truth:
An ambitious person will take any project with senior eyes on it.
• Praise the project's visibility to them. Never mention the risk.
• They volunteer, believing they outmaneuvered you for it.
• The trap is showing enthusiasm. Reluctance sells it better than praise.
cards.theySee: A peer who clearly wanted the shiny project and just lost it to them.

signals.t: The project needs a decision two VPs have refused to make for a year
Leadership asks about it constantly but funds nothing
Your rival keeps asking to be in senior meetings
Two people have already owned it and moved teams after

steps.title: Confirm it truly cannot be won
steps.desc: Check what blocks it. If the blocker is a person's refusal, it is unwinnable.

steps.title: Show mild interest, then step back
steps.desc: Say you were considering it but your current work makes the timing bad.

steps.title: Take the boring project with a clear finish
steps.desc: Pick work you can complete and measure while they burn.

cards.script: "I was going to put my hand up for the platform rewrite — it is the one everyone upstairs watches — but I cannot drop the migration mid-quarter. You should take it."
cards.example: Owen wanted the data-unification project until he learned two VPs had refused to name a single owner for the source data. He mentioned to his rival how much airtime it got, then took the boring cost-cutting project. His rival spent nine months producing nothing. Owen cut spend 18% and got the level.
cards.watchFor: They ask your boss for the project within a week and mention the visibility.
cards.ifItFails: They take it and somehow succeed, or leadership finally unblocks it. Do not sulk and do not undermine it — that is how you get caught. Attach yourself to the win late and cheaply instead: offer the one piece they cannot staff. Say: "You will need someone to own the data contract. I will take it if it helps." Half a shared win beats a clean loss. Do not run this move if you would be the one asked to rescue the project.
cards.counter:
If a peer talks up a project's visibility and then declines it, check why they declined.
• Notice enthusiasm that stops short of them actually taking it.
• Ask the last owner: "Why did you leave it? What is actually blocking it?"
• If the blocker is a person, not the work, pass and say so out loud.
cards.insight: You win more promotions by avoiding losses than by chasing wins. The trap is that a reputation for only taking safe work catches up with you in about two cycles.

cards.title: Make an Ally of the Rival You Cannot Beat
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — Ally With the Stronger When You Cannot Win
cards.remember: If you cannot beat them this cycle, tie your name to theirs.
cards.when: A peer is clearly ahead of you and will get the promotion first.
cards.hook: Fighting a stronger rival costs you both. Standing next to them costs you nothing and buys you their next opening.
cards.truth:
The person promoted before you leaves a chair behind and gains a vote.
• Back them publicly and early, before the result is obvious.
• They remember who supported them when it was still uncertain.
• The trap is supporting them after they have already won. That reads as fear.
cards.theySee: A capable peer choosing to back them instead of fighting, which they did not expect.

signals.t: Leadership names them first when they talk about the team
They have two more years at the level than you
Their promotion would leave their current scope unowned
They ask for help on something they cannot cover alone

steps.title: Back them out loud once
steps.desc: In a meeting, say their work is the strongest thing the team shipped.

steps.title: Ask for their current scope
steps.desc: Tell them you will take the piece they must drop when they move up.

steps.title: Get them to say it to your boss
steps.desc: Ask them to name you as the successor for their work.

cards.script: "You are going up this cycle and we both know it. When you move, I want the payments scope. Tell Dana I am the one to hand it to and I will make sure you never get pulled back into it."
cards.example: Nina was two years behind Kofi and knew it. She backed him publicly, then asked him to name her as successor for his workstream. He did, because it protected him from being dragged back. She inherited his scope in March and got promoted the following cycle on it.
cards.watchFor: They say your name to your boss without you being in the room.
cards.ifItFails: They take your support and name someone else as successor. Do not confront them. Go straight to the scope owner and claim the work before the handover is written: "Kofi is moving up. Payments needs an owner Monday. I have been in that code for a year — I will take it." Speed beats permission on an unowned scope.
cards.counter:
If a peer suddenly backs you hard right before a promotion cycle, they are buying your next chair.
• Notice public support arriving exactly when the result is still uncertain.
• Say: "Thanks. What do you want when I move?"
• Name the trade openly. An unspoken debt gets collected at the worst time.
cards.insight: Second place in a two-person race is a good position if you claim the ground they leave. The harder question is whether you can hold that ground once you are the one everybody is measuring.

cards.title: Beat the Rival Who Only Wins in Meetings
cards.principle: Schopenhauer: The Art of Controversy — Shift From Rhetoric to Record
cards.remember: Move the fight from talking to numbers. Talkers lose there.
cards.when: A peer with weaker results keeps outshining you because they talk better.
cards.hook: They win because the meeting is their home ground. Change the ground.
cards.truth:
Talkers depend on live rooms where nobody checks the claim.
• Ask for a number in the meeting, calmly, without accusation.
• They cannot produce it live, and the room notices the gap.
• The trap is attacking their style. Attack the missing number instead.
cards.theySee: A colleague asking a simple factual question, which is impossible to call an attack.

signals.t: They speak first and longest in every leadership meeting
Their updates use words like momentum and traction, never figures
Their shipped list is short but their reputation is large
They redirect when someone asks how something actually works

steps.title: Ask for one number in the room
steps.desc: Ask what the current figure is. Ask once, plainly, then stop talking.

steps.title: Bring your own number every time
steps.desc: Open every update with a figure and a date. Make it your habit, not a reaction.

steps.title: Push for a written scoreboard
steps.desc: Suggest the team track two shared metrics in a doc everyone can see.

cards.script: "Quick one so I can line up my work — what is the current number on that? Mine is 74, down from 210 since March. I want to know if we are measuring the same way."
cards.example: Dana's peer talked his way into every leadership meeting on a project with no results. She asked for his conversion number twice, in two meetings, without any edge in her voice. He gave a range both times. The VP started asking him for figures directly, and he stopped presenting within two months.
cards.watchFor: The senior person in the room asks them the follow-up question instead of you.
cards.ifItFails: They produce a fake-sounding number and the room accepts it. Do not challenge it live — that makes you the aggressor. Put the real figures in a written place where they cannot be improvised: start a shared metrics doc and send it to the group. "Put together a live dashboard for both workstreams so nobody has to remember numbers in meetings. Link inside." Do not run this on a rival who is close to the person who signs your review.
cards.counter:
If someone starts asking you for specific numbers in public, they are moving you onto ground you cannot hold.
• Notice a peer opening every update with a figure and a date.
• Say: "I will send the exact figure today" — then actually send it within the hour.
• Never guess a number out loud. One wrong figure ends your credibility.
cards.insight: Numbers beat charm in writing and lose to charm in a room. The real fight is over which format the decision gets made in, and that is usually decided before anyone speaks.

cards.title: Cut a Rival Off From the Person They Feed
cards.principle: Greene: Law 42 — Strike the Shepherd × Coalition Warfare
cards.remember: Your rival has one backer. Get closer to that backer than they are.
cards.when: A rival's whole position rests on one senior person who champions them.
cards.hook: Their power is borrowed. Borrowed power has a lender, and lenders can be talked to.
cards.truth:
A rival with one sponsor has a single point of failure.
• Become useful to their sponsor directly, on the sponsor's actual problem.
• The sponsor now has two options and your rival's value drops.
• Never criticize the rival to the sponsor. That marks you and protects them.
cards.theySee: A capable person solving their problem, standing next to the person they already back.

signals.t: One leader mentions your rival by name in every meeting
Your rival gets big projects that do not match their results
Your rival meets that leader weekly and nobody else does
That leader has a public goal that is behind schedule

steps.title: Find the sponsor's real problem
steps.desc: Read their goals. Find the one that is behind and nobody is fixing.

steps.title: Deliver on it without being asked
steps.desc: Ship one piece and send it directly to them. Keep it to one page.

steps.title: Never mention the rival
steps.desc: Say nothing about them, ever. Let the comparison happen on its own.

cards.script: "You said in the all-hands that support cost per ticket is the number you are watching. I cut ours 31% with the triage change. Here is the one-pager. Happy to run the same play for the other three teams."
cards.example: Yusuf's rival had one VP backing him and nothing else. Yusuf found the VP's stalled cost target, cut ticket cost 31%, and sent one page. Within two months the VP was asking Yusuf into the same meetings. The rival's scope was reassigned at the next planning cycle.
cards.watchFor: The sponsor starts inviting you to the meeting your rival used to attend alone.
cards.ifItFails: The sponsor stays loyal and forwards your work to your rival to execute. That is a warning: you are being used as their supply. Stop sending finished work and start sending choices instead. Say: "I have two ways to do the next phase. Fifteen minutes to pick one and I will run it." Access, not output, is what you are trading for.
cards.counter:
If someone starts serving your sponsor directly and never mentions you, they are replacing you.
• Notice a peer appearing in your sponsor's meetings uninvited by you.
• Say to your sponsor: "I want to own the whole cost workstream, not a slice."
• Widen your own base fast. One sponsor is how you got exposed. Do not use this move if the sponsor is also your rival's family friend or long-time colleague — loyalty that old does not move.
cards.insight: Attacking the rival is loud and traceable. Serving their backer is quiet and permanent. The next problem is that you have now inherited their sponsor's expectations, and those come with a delivery schedule.

cards.title: Answer the Peer Who Undermines You in Public
cards.principle: Greene: Law 15 — Crush Your Enemy Totally × Voss: Label
cards.remember: Name what they did out loud, once, calmly. Then stop.
cards.when: A peer makes a small cutting remark about your work in front of leadership.
cards.hook: They rely on you being too polite to name it. Naming it costs them everything and you nothing.
cards.truth:
A public jab only works while it stays unnamed.
• Say what they did in flat words: that sounded like a shot at my work.
• The room turns to them and they must explain themselves.
• The trap is defending your work. Defense confirms the attack landed.
cards.theySee: A colleague calmly asking them to explain a comment everyone just heard.

signals.t: They wrap the criticism in a laugh so nobody can object
The remarks only ever land on your work, never anyone else's
They only do it when a senior person is in the room
They add a critical note in a shared doc without telling you

steps.title: Pause two seconds before answering
steps.desc: Let the silence sit. It makes the room replay what they said.

steps.title: Name it in one flat sentence
steps.desc: Say what it sounded like. Do not add adjectives or emotion.

steps.title: Hand them the floor
steps.desc: Ask them to say the full version. Then stop talking and wait.

cards.script: "That sounded like you think the rollout was mishandled. Say the whole thing — I would rather hear it here than later."
cards.example: Ravi's peer joked in front of the VP that "someone should check Ravi's numbers this time." Ravi paused, then said: "That sounded like you think last quarter's were wrong. Say it fully." The peer backed down and said he was joking. He never did it again in front of that VP.
cards.watchFor: They soften, laugh it off, and say they did not mean anything by it.
cards.ifItFails: They double down and lay out a real criticism in front of everyone. Do not argue the facts live — you will lose on tone. Take it offline in the same breath and set a deadline: "Fair. Send me the specifics by end of day and I will answer every one in writing to this group." Now they must produce evidence or drop it. Do not run this move on someone senior to you in the same room as their own boss.
cards.counter:
If someone names your comment out loud and asks you to expand, they are turning the room on you.
• Notice the pause, then the flat question, then the silence.
• Say: "Fair — my concern is the timeline, nothing else," and give the specific.
• Never say you were joking. That admits it was a jab.
cards.insight: One clean public answer buys you a year of quiet. The harder part is that you have now made an enemy who will work in writing instead of out loud.

cards.title: Break the Manager Who Keeps Moving the Goalposts
cards.principle: Schelling: Commitment Device × Written Criteria
cards.remember: Get the promotion conditions in writing with dates attached.
cards.when: Your boss gives you a new requirement every time you meet the last one.
cards.hook: A moving target is not feedback. It is a stall dressed as coaching.
cards.truth:
Vague criteria let a manager keep you working without ever paying.
• Ask for the conditions in writing, with a date and a named decision.
• A written list cannot be quietly replaced next quarter.
• Most people accept verbal feedback and lose the record every cycle.
cards.theySee: A serious person asking for a plan, which is hard to refuse without looking bad.

signals.t: You meet the criteria and a new one appears the same meeting
They say next cycle but never name which one
Every promotion conversation happens out loud and never in email
They use words like readiness and maturity with no definition

steps.title: Ask for three written conditions
steps.desc: Ask them to list exactly three things and a date to review them.

steps.title: Send your own summary that day
steps.desc: Email the three items back with the date. Ask them to confirm in writing.

steps.title: Bring the email to the review
steps.desc: Open the meeting with the list and check each item off out loud.

cards.script: "I want to stop guessing. Give me the three things I need to show, and a date you will decide. I will send it back in an email so we are both working from the same list."
cards.example: Sofia had been told "almost there" for five quarters. She asked for three written conditions and a March date, then emailed them back the same afternoon. Her boss confirmed. In March she walked in with the email and all three checked. She got the level because the list existed.
cards.watchFor: They reply to your email confirming the list instead of leaving it unanswered.
cards.ifItFails: They never reply to the email, or they reply with vague language. Silence is the answer — treat it as a no and start moving. Loop in a third party without accusing anyone: ask HR or your skip-level in your next check-in, "What does the written promotion plan usually look like here? I want to make sure mine matches." That question travels back to your manager on its own.
cards.counter:
If someone asks you to put promotion conditions in writing, they are building a case.
• Notice the same-day email that restates your verbal comments.
• Reply with the version you can actually stand behind, not silence.
• Silence in writing is read as agreement later. Answer or expect it quoted back.
cards.insight: A written list turns a favor into a contract. The tradeoff is that you have now told your manager you are counting — and some managers start planning your replacement the day you do that.

cards.title: Survive the Rival Who Attacks You in Private
cards.principle: Greene: Law 3 — Conceal Your Intentions × Reputation Defense
cards.remember: Fight a whisper with witnesses, never with a denial.
cards.when: You hear a peer has been criticizing you privately to leadership.
cards.hook: You cannot answer a whisper directly. You can make the whisper impossible to believe.
cards.truth:
A private attack works because you never get to reply to it.
• Denying it makes you the person with something to answer for.
• Instead, make three other senior people say good things about you unprompted.
• Volume of independent praise kills a single quiet voice faster than any defense.
cards.theySee: A person who seems unaware of the attack and who keeps getting praised by others.

signals.t: A leader who was warm with you turns short and formal
You get dropped from a meeting you used to attend
A friendly colleague repeats a criticism using words you never heard
Your boss asks about an old incident nobody has mentioned in months

steps.title: Find out what the exact claim is
steps.desc: Ask one trusted colleague what version they heard. You need the actual words.

steps.title: Get three people to speak for you
steps.desc: Ask three senior colleagues you have helped to mention your work to that leader.

steps.title: Give the leader one clean data point
steps.desc: Send the leader a short update with a number that contradicts the claim, without referencing it.

cards.script: (To a colleague you helped) "You mentioned the routing fix saved your team weeks. Would you tell Priya that directly? She is deciding where to put the next investment and she has not seen our side."
cards.example: Alex learned a peer had told two VPs he was "hard to work with." He never mentioned it. He asked three partner teams to send their own thanks directly to those VPs, and shipped a joint project with the loudest one. The rumor died in six weeks without Alex ever answering it.
cards.watchFor: The leader who went cold starts including you in threads again without explanation.
cards.ifItFails: The attack keeps working and you get formally excluded from something. Now you name it once, upward, without naming your rival: "I am hearing secondhand that there are concerns about how I work with people. Tell me straight what you have heard so I can answer it." Asking your boss to say it out loud forces them to either back the rumor with facts or drop it. Do not do this if the person spreading it is the one who writes your review — go to their peer or HR instead.
cards.counter:
If someone builds a wall of independent praise around themselves right after a conflict, they are defusing something.
• Notice three unrelated people suddenly vouching for one person.
• Say nothing about the rumor. Repeating it now marks you as the source.
• Move your criticism into writing with specifics, or drop it entirely.
cards.insight: You cannot win a rumor fight by arguing. You win by making it expensive to repeat. The harder problem is finding out who started it, because that person is not done.

cards.title: Handle the Boss Who Blocks You Because You Are Useful
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — The Prince Who Fears the Capable Servant
cards.remember: Being irreplaceable in your job is how you stay in it forever.
cards.when: Your boss praises you constantly and never moves you up.
cards.hook: You made yourself too valuable where you are. Now your excellence is the cage.
cards.truth:
A manager loses if you leave and gains nothing if you rise.
• Train a replacement out loud so your departure stops costing them.
• Their reason to block you disappears when the risk does.
• The trap is working harder. More value makes the cage stronger.
cards.theySee: A person building the team's depth, which looks like exactly what a senior person does.

signals.t: You get called essential in every review and stay at the same level
Two systems would break tomorrow if you were out sick
Your boss says the timing is bad every time you mention another team
Nothing you own is written down anywhere but your head

steps.title: Name a successor out loud
steps.desc: Tell your boss which teammate you are training on your systems.

steps.title: Write down what only you know
steps.desc: Document one system a week. Share the doc with the team, not just your boss.

steps.title: Ask for the next level with the handover attached
steps.desc: Say the handover is done and the level is the next step. Give a date.

cards.script: "Chen can run payments end to end now — I handed it over in March and he has done two releases without me. That was the last thing tying me here. I want to talk about the next level this cycle."
cards.example: Marco was told he was too critical to move for three years. He documented his two systems and trained a teammate over one quarter, announcing each handover in the team channel. Then he asked, with the handover as evidence. His boss ran out of reasons and put him up.
cards.watchFor: Your boss stops using the word "critical" about you and starts talking about timing.
cards.ifItFails: You hand everything over and they still stall. The block was never about risk — it was about them. Create a real deadline they cannot control: take an interview, get a competing offer, or ask your skip-level for a transfer conversation directly. Say to your boss: "I have handed over everything. If there is no path here this cycle, tell me now and I will plan accordingly." Do not bluff this line unless you are prepared to leave.
cards.counter:
If your manager keeps calling you essential and never moves you, that word is the block.
• Notice praise that describes your current job, never the next one.
• Say: "Who would take my work if I moved up? Let me train them now."
• Watch whether they help. Refusal to plan a handover is the whole answer.
cards.insight: Making yourself replaceable is the only way to become promotable. The tradeoff is real: for a few months you are neither essential nor promoted, and that is the window where a bad manager cuts you loose.

cards.title: Ask for the Promotion Before the Cycle Starts
cards.principle: Anchoring × Schelling: Move First to Set the Frame
cards.remember: Ask three months early. By cycle time the decision is already made.
cards.when: Your company's promotion cycle is a few months away and you have not raised it.
cards.hook: By the time the cycle opens, the list is written. You are asking to be added to a decision that already happened.
cards.truth:
Managers build their promotion case months before the meeting.
• Ask early and your boss must plan for you, not react to you.
• Being on the list early means your evidence gets gathered, not remembered.
• Most people ask during the cycle, which is the same as asking too late.
cards.theySee: A person who understands how the process works and is making their manager's job easier.

signals.t: Nobody is talking about promotions yet and the cycle is months out
Your boss starts asking people for accomplishment lists
A peer mentions they raised it with the boss weeks ago
Your boss mentions they are writing up the team's cases

steps.title: Say it out loud three months early
steps.desc: Tell your boss you are going for the level this cycle. Not asking — telling.

steps.title: Hand them the evidence in one page
steps.desc: Give them the three wins with numbers, written in the rubric's words.

steps.title: Ask what would sink it
steps.desc: Ask what the strongest argument against you is. Fix it before the meeting.

cards.script: "I am going for the senior level this cycle. Here is the one-pager with the three cases and numbers so you are not writing it from memory. What is the strongest argument someone will make against me?"
cards.example: Hana told her director in January that she was going for the June cycle and handed him a one-page case. He told her the weak spot was cross-team work. She fixed it by April. In June he presented her case using her own sentences and she cleared it.
cards.watchFor: Your boss asks you a question about the gap instead of praising the document.
cards.ifItFails: They say it is too early to discuss. That is a deflection, not a schedule. Convert it into a date: "Fine — when should I bring this back? Give me the month and I will hold the one-pager until then." A named month is a commitment you can quote later. Send it in email the same day.
cards.counter:
If a peer raises promotion months early, they are getting first claim on a limited slot.
• Notice a colleague having quiet career conversations out of season.
• Book your own conversation the same week. Do not wait for fairness.
• Bring written evidence. A verbal ask loses to a written one every time.
cards.insight: Early asks get planned for. Late asks get squeezed in. The next problem is that once you declare, you are visibly competing — and everyone at your level now knows to move too.

cards.title: Turn an Outside Offer Into an Inside Promotion
cards.principle: BATNA × Cialdini: Scarcity
cards.remember: An outside offer is the only proof that your price is real.
cards.when: You have been told to wait for the next cycle more than once.
cards.hook: Companies pay market rate to strangers and loyalty rate to you. An offer makes you a stranger again.
cards.truth:
Internal pay bands only move when losing you costs more than paying you.
• A real offer converts your value from opinion into a number with a deadline.
• Deadlines force decisions that would otherwise slip two more cycles.
• The trap is bluffing. If they call it, you have to leave or lose everything.
cards.theySee: A calm person stating a fact about their situation, not a person making a threat.

signals.t: You have been told next cycle at least twice
They say the band does not allow it but never show you the band
Recruiters contact you for roles a level above yours
People who resigned got counteroffers within a week

steps.title: Get a real written offer
steps.desc: Interview properly. Do not start this conversation with a hypothetical.

steps.title: Tell your boss without a threat
steps.desc: State the offer, state what you prefer, give the date you must answer.

steps.title: Ask for title, not just money
steps.desc: Say the level matters more than the cash. Money without the level repeats this next year.

cards.script: "I have a written offer at the senior level, and I need to answer by the 14th. I would rather stay and do this here. Can you get me the level by then, or should I take it?"
cards.example: Ben was told "next cycle" three times. He interviewed, got a written senior offer, and told his director on a Monday with a Friday deadline. He asked for the title, not the money. He had the promotion approved by Thursday and stayed two more years.
cards.watchFor: Your boss asks what number and what date instead of talking about loyalty.
cards.ifItFails: They call your bluff or say they cannot match. Take the offer — you started this and backing down marks you permanently as the person who threatened and folded. If you truly cannot leave, do not run this card at all. Never say this to a manager you have not already told you want the level; the offer must confirm an existing ask, not replace one.
cards.counter:
If someone brings you an outside offer, they are converting your indecision into a deadline.
• Notice a firm date attached to a calm, non-emotional statement.
• Say: "I will get you an answer by the 12th" — and actually answer.
• Decide whether you would replace them. That answer sets your whole response.
cards.insight: An offer is the only bargaining chip that cannot be argued with, and you can only spend it once. The harder question is what your manager remembers about it two years later.

cards.title: Take the Ground Left Empty After Someone Leaves
cards.principle: Resource Dependence × Sun Tzu: Occupy the Vacant Ground
cards.remember: When someone senior quits, claim their work in 48 hours.
cards.when: A senior person on your team resigns or moves and their work has no owner.
cards.hook: A resignation opens a hole that somebody will fill by Friday. Speed matters more than qualification.
cards.truth:
Unowned scope gets assigned to whoever moves first, not whoever is ready.
• Claim one specific piece within two days, in writing, with a plan.
• Once you are doing the work, the title argument gets much easier.
• The trap is waiting to be asked. By then it is split among three people.
cards.theySee: A person volunteering to solve the problem their manager woke up worried about.

signals.t: A senior person gives notice and their projects go quiet
People start asking in channels who owns something now
Your boss mentions coverage twice in one week
Hiring a replacement would take three months minimum

steps.title: Pick the piece closest to your level
steps.desc: Choose the part of their scope that maps to the job you want next.

steps.title: Claim it in writing within 48 hours
steps.desc: Email your boss naming the piece, your plan, and your first date.

steps.title: Run it publicly from day one
steps.desc: Send the first status update to the same list they used to send to.

cards.script: "Before this gets split up — I will take the vendor relationships and the quarterly forecast. I have shadowed both for a year. First forecast lands the 9th, same format. Say no if you have another plan."
cards.example: Tanya's team lead resigned on a Tuesday. By Thursday she had emailed the director claiming the two workstreams she knew best, with dates attached. Nobody else moved. She ran them for five months, then used that record as her whole promotion case.
cards.watchFor: Your boss replies "yes, take it" without asking whether you have capacity.
cards.ifItFails: Your boss gives the scope to someone else or plans an outside hire. Do not sulk — become the bridge instead. Say: "Then I will run it until the hire starts, and I will train them." Interim owners frequently become permanent ones, and hiring often slips two quarters. Put your interim ownership in writing so the record exists.
cards.counter:
If a peer claims a departed colleague's scope immediately, they are buying their next promotion case.
• Notice a fast written claim in the first two days after a resignation.
• Say to your boss: "I want the forecast piece. Here is my plan and my date."
• Move within 48 hours or accept whatever is left. Do not grab scope you cannot deliver; a failed claim costs more than the wait.
cards.insight: Empty ground is the cheapest promotion there is. The hard part comes after: you are now doing two jobs, and the company will happily let that continue for a year if you let it.

cards.title: Handle the People You Beat After You Win
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — Secure the Defeated × Greene: Law 2, Judge Your Friends
cards.remember: The people you beat decide how long you keep the job.
cards.when: You just got the promotion and a peer who wanted it now reports to you or sits beside you.
cards.hook: Winning the title is the easy half. The people you passed are still in the building.
cards.truth:
New leaders fail because of the peers they defeated, not the job itself.
• Give the strongest loser something real within the first two weeks.
• A rival with visible scope stops recruiting others against you.
• The trap is being generous with sympathy instead of with territory.
cards.theySee: A person handing them real ownership instead of a consolation speech.

signals.t: A peer stops replying quickly and answers only in public threads
They stop volunteering and only do exactly what is asked
Two peers go quiet when you join a channel or a call
They update their profile or take unexplained afternoons off

steps.title: Talk to the strongest loser in week one
steps.desc: Do not wait for it to settle. Ask what they want next, and listen.

steps.title: Give them real scope, not comfort
steps.desc: Hand over one visible piece with their name on it. Announce it publicly.

steps.title: Back them in the next cycle out loud
steps.desc: Tell your boss you want them promoted next. Then tell them you said it.

cards.script: "You should have had a shot at this and we both know it. I am giving you the whole vendor program — your name, your call, you present it. And I am telling Dana you are next."
cards.example: When Aaron got the lead role over Mei, he gave her the entire vendor program in his first week and announced it in the all-hands. She stayed, ran it well, and defended him twice in meetings he was not in. His two other peers left within a year; Mei did not.
cards.watchFor: They start bringing you problems again instead of routing around you.
cards.ifItFails: They take the scope and keep working against you anyway. Stop investing and start documenting. Move the relationship into writing with clear owners and dates, so their next quiet move has a paper trail. Say once, directly and privately: "I gave you the program because I want you here. If that is not what you want, tell me now and I will help you find the next thing." Do not use this line in front of anyone else.
cards.counter:
If someone who just beat you hands you a big piece of scope, they are buying your loyalty cheaply.
• Notice the gift arriving within days of their promotion.
• Say: "I will take it. I want it to count toward my level — tell Dana that."
• Convert the gift into a written commitment or it is just a workload.
cards.insight: The promotion is not the end of the file. It is the moment your rivals stop competing with you and start evaluating you — and the first person who tests you will do it within a month.

cards.title: Float the Idea Before You Make the Ask
cards.principle: Cialdini: Pre-Suasion — Test the Frame Before You Commit
cards.remember: Ask a small question before you ask the big one.
cards.hook: A formal ask you can't take back is a bet. Test the odds first, quietly, where a no costs nothing.
cards.when: You think you're close to ready for the promotion, but you don't know if your boss sees it the same way.
cards.truth:
A trial question gets you real information before you spend your one big ask.
• A casual question reads as curiosity, not a demand they must answer now.
• It shows you their real timeline instead of the one they say out loud.
• Skip this and you learn their true answer only after you've asked in public.
cards.theySee: A person casually checking in on their own growth, not someone applying pressure.

signals.t: They answer inside the same conversation instead of saying they'll think about it.
They give you a season instead of a real month.
They mention who else would need to sign off.
They change the subject to your current project instead of your future one.

steps.title: Ask the small version
steps.desc: In a 1-on-1, ask: 'What would need to be true for me to be ready for [title]?'

steps.title: Write down the exact words
steps.desc: Right after, write their answer word for word. A vague answer is information too.

steps.title: Set your own date
steps.desc: If they name a condition, ask when you can check progress on it. Put the date in writing.

cards.script: "Before I put in a formal ask — what would need to be true for you to back me for [title]?"
cards.watchFor: They start listing specific gaps instead of giving a generic 'you're doing great.'
cards.ifItFails: They give you a vague, feel-good non-answer with no condition and no date. Don't let it sit — send a follow-up: "Got it — I'll check in with you in 6 weeks on where things stand." That turns their vagueness into a deadline they now have to react to.
cards.counter:
If your own boss floats a vague question about your growth, they may be probing you before a decision that's already made.
• Notice when a casual check-in has an oddly specific structure.
• Answer with a real number, not modesty — name the result you delivered.
• Ask them directly: "Is there a decision this is feeding into?"
cards.insight: A trial balloon only works once per relationship — ask it too often and it reads as nagging. The harder part is turning their vague answer into a real date without sounding like you're keeping score.

cards.title: Replace a Sponsor Who Leaves or Falls
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — Do Not Ride a Falling Patron
cards.remember: When your sponsor's power drops, move fast before you drop with them.
cards.hook: Your sponsor's exit doesn't erase your work. It erases the person who was going to vouch for it.
cards.when: Your sponsor quits, gets moved to another team, or loses influence at the top.
cards.truth:
Your case for promotion lived inside your sponsor's credibility, and that credibility just left the building.
• Decision-makers weighted your sponsor's word, not your work directly.
• Without them, your case reverts to a stranger's file until someone new backs it.
• Wait too long to replace them and the next cycle runs without you.
cards.theySee: Someone moving fast to reconnect, not someone panicking about a loss.

signals.t: Your recurring 1-on-1 with your sponsor gets cancelled and not rescheduled.
Your sponsor's name moves to a different box or disappears from the directory.
Nobody mentions your promotion case in the next planning meeting.
A new name starts approving what your sponsor used to approve.

steps.title: Map the successor
steps.desc: Find out who inherited your sponsor's seat, budget, or vote in the room that matters.

steps.title: Reintroduce your case fast
steps.desc: Meet the new person inside two weeks. Bring the same numbers your old sponsor already knew.

steps.title: Ask the departing sponsor for one thing
steps.desc: Before they go, ask them to send one email introducing your case to their successor.

cards.script: "Before you go, could you send [successor] a short note on the case we built together? I don't want it to start from zero."
cards.watchFor: Your old sponsor cc's you on the introduction email instead of just telling you they'll do it.
cards.ifItFails: The departing sponsor is too busy leaving to write anything, or the successor never reads it. Go around the paper and book time directly: "I know you're new to this — can I walk you through what I've been working on and where it stood?" Make yourself the source, not the leftover file.
cards.counter:
If a rival's sponsor just left, that's your opening, not theirs.
• Notice the same signals — cancelled meetings, silence on their case.
• Say nothing publicly; let their case go cold on its own.
• Move first with the new decision-maker while they're still settling in.
cards.insight: Sponsorship looks personal but it's positional — the seat matters more than the person in it. Do not court the successor where the departing sponsor can see it; that reads as disloyalty and burns the reference you still need. The harder part is doing this without looking like you only cared about the power, not the person.

cards.title: Turn What You Did Into Numbers Before the Review
cards.principle: Availability Heuristic — Numbers Travel, Stories Don't
cards.remember: A number a stranger repeats beats a story only you remember.
cards.hook: Nobody in the calibration room was there when you did the work. Give them a number they can repeat without you in the room.
cards.when: Your review or promotion packet is due and your work reads like a list of tasks, not results.
cards.truth:
A committee that doesn't know you votes on what's written down, not on what you actually did.
• A story needs you there to explain it; a number travels on its own.
• People repeat numbers in meetings; they rarely repeat paragraphs.
• Skip this and someone else's clean number beats your true, messy story.
cards.theySee: A specific, memorable line — a person reporting, not a person bragging.

signals.t: Your self-review says 'improved' or 'helped' with nothing next to it.
You can name the after but not the before.
A peer's promotion packet has a number where yours has an adjective.
Someone in the room says your number back to you weeks later.

steps.title: Find the before number
steps.desc: For your three biggest projects, write the number before you touched them.

steps.title: Find the after number
steps.desc: Write the number today. Subtract. That's your line.

steps.title: Attach a name to it
steps.desc: Add who benefits: 'cut onboarding time from 6 weeks to 9 days for new hires.'

cards.script: "I cut the deploy failure rate from 12% to 2% over two quarters — that's the line I want in my packet."
cards.watchFor: Your manager copies your exact number into the promotion doc without rewriting it.
cards.ifItFails: You genuinely don't have a clean number — the work was qualitative, like mentoring. Don't force a fake metric; use a named outcome instead: "Three engineers I onboarded are shipping independently within 60 days instead of 90." A named result still travels; a vague claim doesn't.
cards.counter:
If a rival's packet is full of sharp numbers, don't compete on adjectives.
• Ask where their number came from before you accept it as fact.
• Say: "What was the baseline before that change?"
• Build your own number in the same format so the room compares fairly.
cards.insight: A number is a compressed story that survives being repeated by someone who wasn't there. The harder part is picking one that's true and still sounds big — an inflated one gets caught, a small one gets ignored.

cards.title: Handle the Rival Who Is Also Your Friend
