cards.principle: Greene: Law 15, Softened — Compete Without Crushing When the Relationship Outlasts the Race
cards.remember: Fight for the job. Don't fight for the friendship's ending.
cards.hook: One of you gets the title. Only one of you needs to lose the friendship too — and that part is optional.
cards.when: You and a close friend are both up for the same promotion or the same slot.
cards.truth:
Most people either go soft and lose the job, or go hard and lose the friend — both are avoidable.
• The job and the friendship run on different rules; mixing them loses both.
• Silence about the competition breeds worse resentment than naming it does.
• A friend who feels blindsided later becomes an enemy who knows your weak spots.
cards.theySee: Someone who named the awkward thing out loud instead of pretending it isn't happening.

signals.t: You both stop mentioning the promotion cycle around each other.
One of you jokes about 'may the best person win' more than once.
Your friend stops sharing what they hear through their own channels.
Other people ask you who you think will get it.

steps.title: Name it directly, once
steps.desc: Say plainly you're both in the running and you want to handle it like adults.

steps.title: Set one rule together
steps.desc: Agree out loud: no bad-mouthing each other to the decision-makers, win or lose.

steps.title: Decide the after, before the after
steps.desc: Agree now how you'll act toward each other the day the decision comes out.

cards.script: "We're both up for this. I don't want to pretend it's not happening, and I don't want it to mess up us. Can we agree neither of us plays dirty here?"
cards.watchFor: They visibly relax and agree to the same terms instead of deflecting with a joke.
cards.ifItFails: They deny there's any competition at all, or agree in words but quietly undercut you to a decision-maker anyway. Stop relying on the informal agreement and confirm it directly, once: "I heard you told Sam I'm not ready. I thought we agreed not to do that — what happened?"
cards.counter:
If a friend proposes this 'let's keep it clean' talk, take the deal — but verify it.
• Notice if they ask for the deal right after they hear you're ahead.
• Say yes to the terms, and hold them to it like you'd hold anyone.
• Watch what they do with decision-makers, not just what they say to you.
cards.insight: Do not try this with a friend who already has a reputation for playing dirty — naming a deal only works if they'll honor it. Most damage between friends happens in the silence before the decision, not after. The harder part is honoring the deal when you win and they don't.

cards.title: Contain a Public Mistake Before It Defines You
cards.principle: Greene: Law 5 — Reputation Repair Through Speed, Not Silence
cards.remember: Name the mistake yourself before someone else names it for you.
cards.hook: One bad demo doesn't kill a promotion case. Three weeks of silence about it does.
cards.when: You make a visible mistake — a bad demo, a missed deadline, a wrong call — during your promotion window.
cards.truth:
A mistake becomes a character flaw only if you let someone else write the story of it.
• People remember the last version of the story they heard, not the first.
• Silence reads as denial or not caring — both cost more than the mistake did.
• A fast, factual account of the fix closes the story before it spreads.
cards.theySee: Someone in control of the situation, not someone hiding from it.

signals.t: People who weren't in the room already know a version of what happened.
Your sponsor hasn't mentioned it directly, meaning they heard it from someone else first.
The version you hear back is worse than what actually happened.
You stop getting invited to the kind of meeting where the mistake happened.

steps.title: Tell your sponsor within 24 hours
steps.desc: Go to them with the facts before they hear a worse version elsewhere.

steps.title: Separate the fact from the fix
steps.desc: State what went wrong in one sentence, then what you already changed in the next.

steps.title: Ask for one visible next chance
steps.desc: Request a small, watched task where you can show the fix worked.

cards.script: "I want you to hear this from me first: the demo failed because I skipped the load test. I've already added it to the checklist for every release going forward."
cards.watchFor: Your sponsor asks about the fix instead of the failure — that means the story already moved on.
cards.ifItFails: The story keeps spreading anyway, distorted, and people start treating it as a pattern. Stop correcting the rumor mill directly — repeating it just links your name to the mistake again. Instead, ask for a visible task and let a clean result overwrite the old one: "Put me on [visible task] — I want the next thing people hear about me to be this."
cards.counter:
If a rival is doing damage control on their own mistake, don't help spread the old version.
• Notice when someone keeps re-raising a mistake they've already owned.
• Say nothing that re-tells the story — that does their damage for them.
• If asked directly, give the neutral, current version: "They caught it and fixed it."
cards.insight: Do not use this if the mistake harmed someone else's work directly — own that separately and in person, not as reputation management. The mistake rarely costs the promotion; the untold version people build in the silence does.

cards.title: Spot the Ally Who Reports Your Moves to Your Rival
cards.principle: Sun Tzu: The Use of Spies — Find the Doubled Agent in Your Own Camp
cards.remember: Someone close to you is telling your rival what you say.
cards.hook: Your rival keeps answering things before you've said them out loud. That's not luck. That's a leak.
cards.when: Your rival seems to know your plans, your timeline, or your private complaints before you've told them yourself.
cards.truth:
A promotion fight has a spy in it more often than people admit, usually someone who owes both sides something.
• People who float between two camps trade information as their price of entry to both.
• The leak isn't usually malicious — it's someone who treats gossip as currency.
• Confront the wrong person and you just taught the real leak to be careful.
cards.theySee: Nothing — that's the point. A careful leak looks like a normal friendly coworker.

signals.t: Your rival's move follows your private conversation by a day or two, every time.
Your rival uses a phrase you only said to one person.
The same person shows up in both your inner circle and your rival's.
Someone asks oddly specific questions about your plans right before your rival acts.

steps.title: Run a canary test
steps.desc: Tell a slightly different version of your plan to each suspect. Watch which version reaches your rival.

steps.title: Cut the flow, not the person
steps.desc: Stop sharing real information with the suspect. Keep the relationship normal on the surface.

steps.title: Feed a false detail if you need proof
steps.desc: Give the suspect one false detail. If it reaches your rival, you have your answer.

cards.script: "Hey, off the record — I'm thinking about pushing for the Denver project instead of the platform rebuild. Still deciding." (Say a different false detail to each suspect and watch which one comes back.)
cards.watchFor: Your rival mentions the exact false detail you planted with only one person.
cards.ifItFails: The canary test comes back clean, or the leak stops the moment you get suspicious — which just means they got more careful. Don't accuse anyone without proof. Permanently downgrade what you share instead: real plans go to your sponsor and one trusted peer only, nobody else, from now on.
cards.counter:
If someone runs a canary test on you by feeding you an oddly specific detail, don't repeat it anywhere.
• Notice when gossip feels clean and specific, like it was built to be traced.
• Say nothing about it to anyone until you know where it came from.
• Ask the source directly: "Why are you telling me this?"
cards.insight: Do not accuse anyone based on a single coincidence — a wrongly accused ally becomes a real enemy overnight. Every camp has more leaks than sponsors, because information is cheaper to trade than loyalty is to earn.

cards.title: Get the Real Reason When They Say Not Yet
cards.principle: Voss: Label — Turn a Canned Rejection Into a Real Answer
cards.remember: A vague no hides the real reason. Push for it.
cards.hook: 'Not this cycle' is not an answer. It's a sentence built to end the conversation, not inform you.
cards.when: You're told you didn't get the promotion, with a vague or generic reason attached.
cards.truth:
Managers give a soft, generic reason because it's easier than the specific, awkward truth.
• A vague reason protects them from a hard conversation, not you from bad news.
• The real reason is usually one of three things: budget, politics, or one named gap.
• Accept the vague version and you'll spend a year fixing the wrong thing.
cards.theySee: Someone taking the news professionally, not someone about to make it their problem.

signals.t: They use words like 'timing' or 'not quite yet' with nothing attached.
They look at their notes more than at you while delivering it.
They try to close the meeting right after telling you.
They don't offer you a plan or a date for the next attempt.

steps.title: Let the first answer land, then ask again
steps.desc: Say you appreciate the honesty, then ask directly for the specific reason.

steps.title: Ask for the vote, not the vibe
steps.desc: Ask what specifically came up in the room, not how they personally feel about you.

steps.title: Get one written condition
steps.desc: Ask them to put the one thing you need to fix in writing, with a check-in date.

cards.script: "I appreciate you telling me straight. Before I take that at face value — what specifically came up in the room that I should know about?"
cards.watchFor: They pause, then name one real, specific thing instead of repeating the vague version.
cards.ifItFails: They repeat the same vague line a second time, refusing to get specific. Stop asking them and go around: ask your sponsor separately, since they may have heard the real reason in the room you weren't in. Say to your sponsor: "I got a generic answer from my manager — did you hear what actually came up?"
cards.counter:
If you're the one delivering a vague 'not this cycle,' expect this pushback.
• Notice when your generic reason doesn't satisfy them — that's fair, not overreach.
• Have the specific reason ready before the meeting.
• If there truly isn't one, say that plainly: "It came down to budget, not you."
cards.insight: Do not push for the real reason in the same meeting if you're visibly upset — come back in a day and ask calmly instead. The vague no is designed to close a conversation, and pushing past it is the only way to get something you can act on.

cards.title: Negotiate the Pay to Match the Title
cards.principle: Anchoring × Cialdini: Consistency — Close the Gap Between the New Title and the Old Number
cards.remember: A new title with old pay is a discount, not a win.
cards.hook: They'll hand you the title fast. The money moves slower unless you make it move.
cards.when: You get the promotion, but the pay bump attached to it is smaller than the market rate for the new title.
cards.truth:
Companies often approve the title change and the smallest number that legally counts as a raise.
• Titles cost the company nothing on paper; money is the part they ration.
• Once you accept the number, it becomes the anchor for every raise after it.
• The window to negotiate is wide open right after the promotion, then shuts fast.
cards.theySee: Someone grateful for the title who's also doing basic homework on the number.

signals.t: The new number sits at the bottom of the range for the new title.
They ask you to sign or confirm within the same conversation.
They don't mention what others at your new title earn.
They say your pay will 'catch up' at the next cycle with no number attached.

steps.title: Find the market number first
steps.desc: Check the going rate for your new title before the pay conversation happens.

steps.title: Say thanks, then ask for the gap
steps.desc: Accept the promotion warmly, then raise the number as its own separate topic.

steps.title: Ask for a number, not a promise
steps.desc: If they can't move now, get a specific number and date in writing for the next review.

cards.script: "Thank you for this — I'm genuinely glad about the title. Separately, I looked at the range for this role and the offer is at the bottom of it. Can we close that gap now?"
cards.watchFor: They go quiet for a moment, then ask what number you had in mind — that means the budget has room.
cards.ifItFails: They say the budget is fixed for this cycle with no room to move. Don't drop it — convert it into a written commitment instead: "Understood. Can we put in writing that my pay gets reviewed against the new band in six months, not at the next annual cycle?"
cards.counter:
If your manager says 'the title is the win, the money will catch up,' recognize the anchor they're setting.
• Notice that 'it'll catch up' never comes with a number or a date.
• Ask directly: "What number, by when?" Silence tells you it's not coming.
• If you're giving the promotion, only promise a date you'll actually keep.
cards.insight: Do not push hard on pay in the same breath as thanking them if the budget freeze is public and company-wide — get the written commitment instead. A title is permanent and cheap to hand out; a raise is recurring and expensive, which is exactly why they're kept separate.

cards.title: Turn Former Peers Into Reports Without Losing the Room
cards.principle: Machiavelli: The Prince — The New Prince Among Old Equals
cards.remember: You changed rank. Change how you enter the room.
cards.hook: Yesterday they were your equal at lunch. Today they wait for you to speak first, whether you meant to change that or not.
cards.when: You get promoted to manage people who were your peers, sometimes including the rival you beat.
cards.truth:
The room re-reads every word you say the day the title changes, even if you don't feel different.
• Peers now watch for favoritism, insecurity, or a power trip in your first small calls.
• The first person you correct or praise sets the pattern everyone else expects.
• Move too fast and you confirm their fear; move too slow and you look unable to run the team.
cards.theySee: Someone acting like a manager on purpose, in small visible choices, not someone performing a role.

signals.t: A former peer jokes to test whether you'll laugh along or act like a boss now.
Someone still cc's you the way they used to cc your old manager, or skips you entirely.
People glance at each other after you make your first call as their manager.
Someone who wanted the job vents to a peer instead of to you directly.

steps.title: Have the direct conversation first
steps.desc: Meet each former peer 1-on-1 before the team meeting where it becomes official.

steps.title: Name the change out loud
steps.desc: Say plainly the working relationship changes even if the respect doesn't.

steps.title: Make your first decision small and fair
steps.desc: Pick a low-stakes call early and make it visibly by-the-rule, not by-the-friendship.

cards.script: "I know this is a change for both of us. I still want your honest take, and I'm going to make some calls you won't always agree with. I'd rather you tell me that directly than let it sit."
cards.watchFor: They test you once with a boundary-pushing comment, then drop it once you hold a clear, calm line.
cards.ifItFails: A former peer keeps treating you like an equal in front of the team, undercutting your calls or venting to others. Address it privately, specifically, and once: "When you pushed back on my call in front of the team, it undercut me. Bring it to me first next time." If it repeats, it becomes a documented performance conversation, not a friendship problem.
cards.counter:
If your new manager is a former peer testing their authority on you, decide fast whether to challenge or fall in line.
• Notice their first small decision and treat it as the real signal.
• If you disagree, say it to them privately, not to the team.
• If they handle it fairly, drop the old peer-level pushback in group settings.
cards.insight: Do not skip the direct one-on-one with the peer you personally beat for the role — skipping it is the fastest way to lose the room. The harder question is what you do with the peer who wanted this more than anyone and now reports to you.

cards.title: Take the Acting Role Without Signing Away the Promotion
cards.principle: Schelling: Commitment Device — Get the Terms Before You Do the Free Work
cards.remember: Get the date and title in writing before you start.
cards.hook: 'Acting director' sounds like a promotion. Without a date attached, it's just a bigger job at the old price.
cards.when: You're offered an interim or acting role covering a bigger title, with promotion talked about but not promised.
cards.truth:
Companies get the output of the bigger role for the price of the smaller one, and 'we'll see how it goes' has no expiration date.
• The interim label lets them test you without spending a title or raise yet.
• The longer you run it well without terms, the more normal free work looks.
• Ask for terms after six months of doing the job and you've lost your leverage.
cards.theySee: Someone confident enough to ask for structure, not someone ungrateful for the opportunity.

signals.t: Nobody names when the 'acting' period ends or gets reviewed.
Nobody tells you what you need to show to make it permanent.
Your paycheck doesn't move even though your responsibilities did.
They describe it as 'let's see how it goes' instead of naming a process.

steps.title: Ask for the criteria before you start
steps.desc: Ask exactly what needs to be true for 'acting' to become permanent.

steps.title: Ask for a review date
steps.desc: Get a specific date, not a season, when the role gets formally reconsidered.

steps.title: Ask for interim pay
steps.desc: Request a stipend or partial bump for the interim period, separate from the final promotion.

cards.script: "I want to do this well. Before I start, can we agree on what 'permanent' looks like and put a review date on the calendar — say, 90 days out?"
cards.watchFor: They give you an actual date and write it down somewhere, instead of just nodding along.
cards.ifItFails: They resist naming a date or criteria, saying it's 'too early to lock in.' Protect yourself in writing on your own terms: send a follow-up email summarizing the conversation. Say: "Confirming what we discussed — I'll take this on, and we'll revisit the permanent title and pay in 90 days." Silence back from them is still a record you can point to later.
cards.counter:
If you're handing someone an acting role with no terms, expect a savvy person to ask for exactly this structure.
• Notice if they ask for a date and criteria; that's a sign they'll do the job well.
• Decide before the offer whether you can actually commit to a review date.
• If you can't commit to terms, say so honestly instead of letting 'we'll see' become the plan.
cards.insight: Do not accept the acting role at all if they refuse even an informal date or stipend — that refusal is a sign the interim label is meant to be permanent. The harder part is asking for structure at the exact moment you're supposed to look grateful.
